name: Chloe Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group without ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers are confidential, including what you say privately. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a four-person carpentry crew fitting out the old Harbour Clinic building, and I still hang the awkward doors myself. By seven I'm marking the door openings, then I'm moving the plumbers and electricians round each other so no one waits all morning. My trade certificate got me into carpentry, but twenty years on site taught me which drawing is lying. The firm's lead rate is low, and the only other fit-out outfit near us pays less.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does the household have to cover each month?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Marco drives a parcel van, and our grown daughters have homes of their own. We still pay two hundred a month on the loan from Marco's failed catering stall, and we've saved about two weeks of bills. I use AI now and then to tidy a client email, but I measure every fire-door gap with a ruler and the approved drawing. A missed week on site would put the loan payment against the heating bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the clever part of a phone won't hang a heavy fire door. If the software only tidies forms, I can live with that, provided we still check the opening on site. I wouldn't ask anyone to buy a new screen for a ten-minute saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, a quiet AI future leaves the old money problem exactly where it is. Our two-week reserve cannot cover a lost site week and Marco's van pay is already irregular in winter. The clinic contract runs to June, but the next signed fit-out has not appeared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking the clinic shifts and check the next contract with our manager at the Friday site meeting. Starting this month, I'd pay twenty extra toward the stall loan only after rent and heating clear, using any paid Saturday hours. I would not call the same cash in another account new savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy when I picture the gap after June. The little AI change is easy; the unsigned next job is not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a one-week gap mean in actual bills?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A week's lost pay would be about four hundred after tax. We have only enough aside for roughly two weeks of ordinary bills, so I'd delay the extra loan payment first and speak to the lender before missing the required one. I won't tell the girls everything is fine if the site closes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does your occasional email tool change the safety check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I let the tool shorten a client note, then I compare every door number with the approved drawing. The fire-door gap gets a ruler, not a confident paragraph. A tidy note is useful, but it cannot sign off the building.

say: I would tell the crew **site measurements** still decide whether a fire door fits.
I would say small software savings are useful only after a **physical check**.
think: The **unsigned next contract** worries me more than AI in this picture.
Our **two-week reserve** leaves little room for a lost site week.
do: Keep the **clinic shifts** and ask the manager about signed work after June.
Pay **twenty extra** on the stall loan only after rent and heating clear.
feel: **Uneasy** about the job gap, though the technology itself feels small.
S0.quote: A tidy note is useful, but it cannot sign off the building.
fieldNote: Her attention returns to the **June contract end**, despite saying the software itself is harmless.
Two weeks of expenses and a fixed **loan payment** make even one missed site week consequential.

steps.text: Keep clinic shifts and ask the manager for signed work after June
Pay twenty extra on the stall loan after rent and heating clear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the site manager to show us a real doorway before trusting a computer's forty-minute allowance. Faster ordering might help when a hinge is missing, but a neat programme can hide a crooked wall. I'd want the crew's correction written into the work order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The planning and checking part of my lead role could shrink while my hands are still needed. If one supervisor watches three sites on a screen, my lead allowance could go before a robot touches a door. Marco's parcel rounds may also get tighter, although vans still need drivers for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd test the new ordering screen on two clinic rooms with the foreman and record where it gets the door sizes wrong. I'd ask in writing whether the lead allowance or paid checking time changes before I accept extra rooms. If paid hours drop for two months, I'd apply to the one nearby renovation contractor, but only for a posted job that covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious rather than surprised. I can learn a proven screen, but I can't learn away a pay cut while the loan is due.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say when the software gives a room forty minutes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the manager to room seven, where the wall bows behind the plaster. My tape says the jamb needs packing, and that's a paid hour before a door can be hung safely. I won't let a computer's number turn that hour into unpaid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What counts as a reason to apply elsewhere?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two short payslips in a row would be my trigger, not a rumour at tea break. I'd want the contractor's posted lead rate, travel costs and guaranteed hours before moving. The nearby firm usually pays less, so an offer has to add up on paper.

say: I would ask for a **room trial** before faster targets become paid crew rules.
I would insist that **checking time** and the lead rate are written down.
think: My **lead allowance** could shrink before robots reach carpentry.
Marco’s **parcel rounds** may tighten, leaving our loan harder to cover.
do: Test **two clinic rooms** against the new ordering screen with the foreman.
Request written terms for **lead pay** and paid checking before accepting new targets.
Apply for a **posted local job** after two short payslips, if its pay covers bills.
S1.quote: I can learn a proven screen, but I can't learn away a pay cut while the loan is due.
fieldNote: She separates her **physical carpentry** from the lead planning allowance that may change earlier.
Her willingness to test software depends on **paid checking time**, not simply access to a tablet.

steps.text: Test two clinic rooms against the ordering screen with the foreman
Request written lead pay and paid checking terms before new targets
Apply for a posted local bill-covering job after two short payslips

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our crew that the thinking system arrives in 2028, while a robot good enough to hang doors follows around 2031. We need the owner to publish who checks the doors and who gets paid for that work. A promise of future robot jobs without a funded place is no plan for a crew of four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My room plans and ordering checks could be done by 2028, so the lead allowance is at risk almost at once. My hands may earn for roughly three more years, but capable robots around 2031 could cut even that work. With two weeks saved and the stall loan outstanding, I cannot bridge a long lost wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd ask the owner for written 2028 staffing and 2031 robot plans, including the lead rate and safety sign-off. I'd take paid weekend fit-out shifts only when they're available and put the extra pay toward the loan. If a verified cut arrives, I'd ask the lender for a revised schedule before the required payment is missed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm alarmed. The first change could hit the lead money before I've built a cushion, and I can see the second one coming down the corridor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you train for robot work during the three-year gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if there's a funded local course, paid time to attend and a posted role with a wage that covers the loan and rent. I won't leave a paid crew for an unpaid demonstration. No one has shown me those terms yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Marco about the two dates?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my husband Marco that route software may change his parcel hours before vans can drive themselves. We'd compare both payslips each month and call the lender if a required payment looks doubtful. We cannot pretend my three years of possible site work are three years of guaranteed wages.

say: I would ask for **written staffing plans** and paid safety sign-off before 2028.
I would tell the crew **site robots** follow thinking AI around 2031.
think: My **lead allowance** could fall in 2028 before physical door work is automated.
Two weeks of savings cannot bridge lost **site wages** after capable robots arrive.
do: Ask the owner for **written dates**, lead pay and safety sign-off terms this month.
Put available **paid weekend wages** toward the stall loan after essentials.
Ask the **lender** for revised payments if a verified cut threatens the next bill.
feel: **Alarmed** by a possible near-term lead-pay cut and later site robots.
S2.quote: We cannot pretend my three years of possible site work are three years of guaranteed wages.
fieldNote: Her first exposure is the paid **lead planning** before robots touch carpentry.
She rejects vague robot training without **funded local places**, paid time and a real bill-covering vacancy.

steps.text: Ask the owner for written lead pay and safety sign-off plans
Pay extra toward the stall loan from available paid weekend shifts
Ask the lender for revised payments if a verified cut threatens bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives a working crew time to see what the company actually buys. Thinking AI in 2031 could take the paperwork, while capable site robots follow around 2034. I'd ask for a yearly explanation of where the paid work will be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the clinic and later contracts hold, the stall loan should be gone before thinking AI arrives. That would remove one fixed bill, but it would not create a pension by itself. I could still lose lead pay in 2031 and fitting hours around 2034, when I'd need real income figures before deciding whether to stop working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the agreed loan instalment and add paid Saturday money when it exists. Once the lender confirms the balance is zero, I'd transfer that former instalment from each new pay packet into a retirement account. I'd ask the union adviser for an actual income estimate at 63 and 66, and keep taking site work unless that estimate covers our costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, but I can see a sequence now. Five years gives me time to clear debt and test the numbers rather than guessing at a finish date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave work at 63 if the loan is gone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. A cleared loan is only one line of the household budget. I'd need the actual retirement income, Marco's likely wages, health costs and rent all on one sheet. If the figures do not cover them, I keep applying for paid site or inspection work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you accept as inspection work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd consider a posted local role that pays enough, gives me authority to stop an unsafe door and funds the training on paid time. If all they offer is a title and unpaid travel, I stay on the tools while I can. A safety signature needs a person who can actually say no.

say: I would ask for **yearly staffing figures** as thinking AI and site robots arrive.
I would keep **safety authority** with the person signing off each door.
think: Clearing the **stall loan** would help, but it would not guarantee retirement income.
My **lead pay** could change in 2031 and fitting hours around 2034.
do: Keep paying the **loan**, adding only available paid Saturday earnings.
Start a new **retirement transfer** from wages after the lender confirms the loan is cleared.
Ask the union adviser for **income estimates** at 63 and 66 before any work exit.
feel: **Anxious**, with more room to plan than in the fast case.
S3.quote: A cleared loan is only one line of the household budget.
fieldNote: She distinguishes debt freedom from an affordable **retirement income**.
Five years lets her seek actual figures, but any work exit remains conditional on **household costs**.

steps.text: Pay the agreed loan instalment and extra from available Saturday wages
Start new retirement transfers after the lender confirms the loan is cleared
Ask the union adviser for actual retirement income estimates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew ten years lets us watch each step instead of buying an expensive promise. Thinking AI comes around 2036, and robots capable of site fitting follow around 2039. I still want every door checked by someone who can refuse a bad installation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I may have stopped climbing by 2039, but only if our actual retirement income pays the rent, food and health bills. At 68 in 2036, I would rather be choosing a finish date than having one forced on me. If the figures fail, I'd need paid work after 2036 and I cannot assume a local inspection post will exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd clear the stall loan on schedule, then make a new monthly retirement transfer from wages rather than just moving old savings. Every year I'd compare the actual pension estimate, Marco's income and our bills with a union adviser. In the first year after 2036, I'd keep paid site checks only if the employer still has them and the work is safe for my knees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy because ten years gives us time but doesn't fill the account by magic. I can handle a plan with dates and figures. A guess about being retired would worry me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if you cannot afford to stop by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask about a posted local quality-checking job, with paid training and the right to reject unsafe work. If there is no funded place at a wage we can live on, I cannot count it as income. Marco and I would adjust spending and keep seeking paid work we can actually do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a robot for the crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't own the firm and I won't borrow against our home for its machine. I'd look at a real field trial and ask who carries the repair and insurance costs. My own job is checking the fitted door, if anyone still pays for that check.

say: I would ask for **field trials** and safety sign-off before site robots arrive.
I would describe retirement as a **household calculation**, not a birthday.
think: I could stop climbing before robots only if **actual retirement income** meets our costs.
If it does not, any **post-2036 work** depends on a real paid opening.
do: Clear the **stall loan** before starting new transfers from wages.
Review actual **retirement income and bills** with the union adviser each year.
Continue paid **site checks** after 2036 only if offered and safe for my knees.
feel: **Uneasy** but able to plan with real figures.
S4.quote: A guess about being retired would worry me.
fieldNote: Ten years gives her time to clear debt and measure **retirement affordability**, without assuming an exit age.
She will not fund the employer’s robot, and treats any later **inspection role** as conditional on a paid opening.

steps.text: Clear the stall loan and begin new retirement transfers from wages
Review actual retirement income and household bills with the union adviser yearly
Continue paid site checks after 2036 only if offered and safe
Seek posted local quality work if shortfall, with funded paid training, rejection authority and bill-covering pay

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the lead money could go in two years and the door work around 2031, before the loan is clear. A written staffing plan, paid local training tied to real jobs, and help with required payments after a verified wage cut would matter. I need safety checks paid for, not just promised.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who decides a door is safe when the machine and the drawings disagree. The person signing the door should have time and the authority to stop the job. My crew cannot eat a nice forecast when the payslip is short.

headlineQuote: My crew cannot eat a nice forecast when the payslip is short.
portrait: Chloe leads a **four-person fit-out crew** and checks doors against drawings with her own measurements.
Her **low lead pay**, two-week reserve and old stall loan make lost paid hours a household threat.
She will try **proven software** with paid checking time, while insisting that site workers can reject unsafe targets.
For later AGI worlds she seeks **actual retirement figures** and keeps working when the numbers do not cover costs.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut Chloe’s lead pay before robots threaten her door-fitting work and before the loan is cleared.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **written staffing plans**, paid local training tied to posted jobs, paid safety checks and help after a verified wage cut.
